items._ogDesc: Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, is looking for someone to manoeuvre the venture’s enormous hunger for energy.
items.body:
Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, is looking for someone to manoeuvre the venture’s enormous hunger for energy.

“We are hiring a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada,” reads the job description.

“Some of our campuses will run on gas-fired, behind-the-meter generation. … If gas does not arrive, in the volume and at the pressure the plant needs, the compute does not run.”

  • Anthropic firm set to begin trading as a US$1.5T company
  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

It’s a high-stakes job – and a considerable salary. A successful candidate could earn up to just over half a million per year, in Canadian dollars (US$320,000 to US$405,000). Energy capacity will define Anthropic’s ability to produce artificial intelligence – a technology that it broadly believes can usher a cure for cancer, or design biological weapons if misused.

Whatever its use, Anthropic’s staffer will need to source a lot of energy. The company predicted earlier this year that the U.S. AI sector will need at least 50 gigawatts of capacity “over the next several years” to operate.

Where will the power come from?

When asked by CTVNews.ca, the company did not provide a prediction for what the Canadian AI sector would need. Canada’s overall generation capacity was just about 156 gigawatts in 2025.

“We all know that AI requires vast amounts of energy, and so the questions that we have are: where will that energy come from? How will it get to these sites? And what will the impact be for the average consumer?” asked Gitane De Silva, former CEO of the Canada Energy Regulator. These days, she’s the executive director of the Peter Lougheed School of Politics and Democracy at the University of Alberta.

“Canada is blessed with every single form of energy out there. We’ve got tremendous oil supplies, gas supplies, wind, solar, all of it,” she said in an interview with CTVNews.ca. Canada also has the fortune of a colder climate, potentially reducing the need to artificially cool data centres. Cooling has historically accounted for 40 per cent of a data centre’s energy suck.

But, she added, if Canada wants to meet the moment, it will need to build up energy sourcing, generation and transportation infrastructure. That could range from something as complex as pipeline capacity or as straightforward as road access to new sites.

Canadian energy: Asset or constraint?

Canada’s official AI strategy calls energy both “an asset and a current constraint.”

“Canada’s grid is among the cleanest in the world, but available power for large-scale AI buildout is limited today,” reads the strategy, which calls Canada “vulnerable” on infrastructure.

But that hasn’t stopped American companies from increasing their footprint across the border. Meta, Mark Zuckerberg’s tech conglomerate that owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is building a $13-billion-plus data centre in Alberta’s Industrial Heartland.

It could be the largest outside the U.S., once finished, and consume one gigawatt of power. It takes about 1.4 gigawatts to power Edmonton.

The company hopes to power it with a bespoke gas plant, which won’t be operational before the data centre is up and running. Meta has rights to connect to Alberta’s grid in the meantime.

Do they have to be gas guzzlers?

Anthropic is hiring a gas supply leader. A gas plant will power Meta’s centre. What about renewable energy?

“The reality is that AI data centres need 100 per cent reliability,” said De Silva. “There’s no point in time when the electricity cannot flow to the centre. And so, that becomes the limitation of renewables. … If the wind is not blowing or the sun is not shining, then there needs to be a backup.”

“The reality is that the world remains very, very addicted to fossil energy, and … consumption is not declining at a rate that would be necessary to meet those climate targets,” she also said.

Posed with that assertion, Martin Karsten, computer science professor at the University of Waterloo, pushed back.

“I would challenge this notion that all these AI services really need all this, sort of, extremely high reliability and availability,” he said.

Karsten contends that there are two principal functions of AI. First, AI companies need to train their models to make them smarter. But that kind of work is “asynchronous,” according to the professor. It “can happen any time of the day.”

On the other hand, there are the queries, when a user inputs a command and the AI model responds with some sort of action, such as analysis, calculations, or media content. Society – as a group of people using AI – must determine how quickly it expects that sort of service.

“If I submit an X-ray for advice, and I get a response within 12 to 24 hours. Are we happy enough? If, of course, I’m on Instagram and watching the cartoons or whatnot … then I need it right away, right?”

For its part, Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a N.S. data centre in collaboration with EverWind Fuels – a wind and green hydrogen developer – according to the Canadian company.

‘Damned’ either way

David Duvenaud, who led a team at Anthropic examining model safety, has called for a moratorium on new model training and increased development transparency.

In an interview with CTVNews.ca, he argued AI’s potential impact on the labour market should raise alarm bells for countries that are looking to integrate it into their economies. On the energy side, he said, Canada finds itself in a difficult position.

“I basically see it as we’re sort of damned if we do and damned if we don’t. In the sense that, if we don’t build a whole bunch of power in data centres, unless there is giant global co-ordinated slowdown, which I think would be a great idea, then the U.S. will just have insane economic growth, and Canada will basically be left in the dust.”

On the other hand, rapid growth could lead to an undesirable downstream effect on labour, should employers opt to replace human workers with AI agents, said Duvenaud.

“If we stay relevant by building tons of power plants and data centres and robot factories, … the relative worth of human capital is just going to go down, and we’ll all just end up either with sinecures or just be dependents of the state forever.”

items._ogDesc: The federal Liberals are expected to face a vote Thursday in the House of Commons on their 2026 budget.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- The federal Liberals are expected to face a vote Thursday in the House of Commons on their 2026 budget.

The budget, tabled Nov. 5, proposes billions of dollars in new borrowing and tax measures largely aimed at stimulating infrastructure construction and other capital projects.

Last year’s budget vote was a tense affair, as the minority Liberal government of the day needed members of other parties to either back its agenda or abstain from the vote to pass the spending plan.

Then-Green Party Leader Elizabeth May offered the crucial vote that allowed Budget 2025 to pass, while two NDP and two Conservative MPs abstained or were absent.

Due to a series of byelections and floor-crossings over the last year, the Liberals now hold a majority of seats in the Commons. That means the government can pass much of its agenda without the support of other parties.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has railed against the scale of the proposed borrowing in the budget, while NDP Leader Avi Lewis argues the Liberals are catering to big business with their latest spending plan.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne claims the budget meets an uncertain moment by leveraging Canada’s relatively strong fiscal position to invest in its future.

Measures like the $36-billion productivity mega-deduction are aimed at trying to convince businesses to invest more in their own machinery and boost worker productivity, while other budget proposals look to support Canada’s cultural sectors and eliminate homelessness.

The budget’s title -- “Maitres Chez Nous,” or “Masters of our Destiny -- borrows a phrase from Quebec’s Quiet Revolution, a period of rapid socio-economic change in the province.

Bloc Quebecois Leader Yves-Francois Blanchet has criticized the Liberals’ use of the phrase, arguing the budget doesn’t give the province more control over its own affairs.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.body:
OTTAWA — Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is set to hold the first meeting of an advisory committee on bilateral economic relations since the midterm elections that delivered a sharp rebuke of the Trump administration.

LeBlanc’s office confirmed the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations will hold a virtual meeting today.

Canadian Ambassador to the United States Mark Wiseman and Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette will also be in attendance.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after trade negotiations broke down in August.

Midterm election exit polling indicated that Trump’s trade war and his sweeping tariff agenda were unpopular with American voters.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

items.title: An early rally for Wall Street evaporates as the market waits for Anthropic’s stock to begin trading
items.description: Buzz around Anthropic’s blockbuster debut on Wall Street is juicing up beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence Thursday and helping the U.S. market recover some of its recent slide.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Anthropic logo is displayed on the Nasdaq MarketSite tower as part of the Anthropic IPO in New York, Thursday, Nov.19, 2026. (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Buzz around Anthropic’s blockbuster debut on Wall Street is juicing up beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence Thursday and helping the U.S. market recover some of its recent slide.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Early-morning optimism on Wall Street is giving way to more sharp swings Thursday as stocks tied to artificial intelligence give back some of their gains made on buzz around Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO.

After rallying 1.3 per cent at the start of trading and appearing set to break its longest losing streak since June, the S&P 500 quickly erased all of it and flipped to a loss of 0.3 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 437 points, or 0.9 per cent, as of 10:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.1 per cent higher.

The wide majority of stocks outside of AI fell, as companies whose fortunes are more closely tied to the strength of the economy struggled. Four out of every five stocks within the S&P 500 index sank.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Williams-Sonoma dropped 9.1 per cent after the retailer reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street’s forecast.

Walmart sank 1.9 per cent even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.

Earlier in the morning, stocks tied to the AI industry seemed to be doing well enough to overshadow all those losses.

They rallied after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold its stock at a price of US$83 each in its initial public offering. That’s more than the US$70 to US$78 that it earlier thought it would get. Its stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq later in the day.

The strong demand for Anthropic’s IPO appeared to show that faith remains among investors about the AI revolution, even though stocks in the industry have been careening recently on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology and were bound to deflate.

But AI stocks quickly returned to their jittery ways and gave back much of the gains as the morning progressed.

Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared because of the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8 per cent before paring its gain to 1.5 per cent.

CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, went from a 10.5 per cent leap to a rise of 1.7 per cent.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Nvidia likewise pared its gain, but it was still up 0.8 per cent and heading toward its first gain in six days. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with worries that have been dogging the entire industry.

At first it was the longstanding criticism that AI stocks had gone into a bubble after shooting so high, along with doubts that AI could produce enough profit and productivity to make the heavy investments in AI data centres worth it. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI.

Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He had been one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while also using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth.

Other stocks in the AI industry, meanwhile, offered some encouraging signals.

Palo Alto Networks climbed 3.7 per cent after the AI cybersecurity company topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also agreed to buy Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, to help customers adopt AI securely in an all-stock deal valued at US$4.5 billion.

Everpure, a company that helps businesses manage and store their data, said its revenue jumped 51 per cent last quarter from a year earlier in part because of AI-related offerings. That was more than analysts expected, as was its profit for the quarter. Everpure’s stock rose 13.9 per cent.

In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady, even though a couple reports on the U.S. economy came in below economists’ expectations. One said slightly more U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, though the number remains relatively low compared with history. Another said manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region is slowing by more than economists expected.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 5.06 per cent from 5.07 per cent late Wednesday.

In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent. Helping to lead the way was SoftBank Group, which climbed 4.6 per cent. It was an early investor in OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and competitor to Anthropic.

South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent thanks to strength for its stocks tied to the AI boom, but indexes were weaker elsewhere in Asia and in Europe.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writer Chan Ho-him contributed.

items._ogDesc: The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is set to begin trading in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is set to begin trading on Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods.

The company priced its initial public offering at US$83 per share, enough to value the entire business at US$1.5 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record.

The higher-than-anticipated price was surprising, given that investor worries have ratcheted up even more in recent days after AI’s chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, was ousted amid a possible Chinese spying scandal.

But the bigger test will be how Anthropic fares in trading.

Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by stockholders. Proceeds totaling US$81 billion put Anthropic’s IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about US$75 billion in June. SpaceX, however, holds a higher valuation, about US$1.9 trillion as of Wednesday.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut on the Nasdaq sometime after the stock market opens under the ticker symbol ANT. The company had earlier set a price range of US$70 to US$78 per share.

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there’s the spectacular downfall of one of the industry’s biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.

The company’s rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year.

IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt

Anthropic already has taken on US$6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.

While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend US$900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including US$70 billion in the next 12 months.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.

Anthropic’s IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.

AI industry faces concerns about data centres, a possible bubble and regulations

Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.

Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.

Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.

In comments at the opening bell Thursday, Amodei sought to dampen fears by stressing a commitment to ensure humans are in control of the technology.

“If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same,” he said. ”The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.”

Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centres, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.

Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.

“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”

Bernard Condon and Barbara Ortutay, The Associated Press

Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

items.title: ‘I mean, I’m not MAGA,’ Elon Musk says after Republicans’ midterm election washout
items.description: After Republicans’ midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world’s richest man insists he’s not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels “pretty foolish” for spending so much money on the cause.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump listens as Elon Musk speaks outside the West Wing of the White House, Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Alex Brandon</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: After Republicans’ midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world’s richest man insists he’s not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels “pretty foolish” for spending so much money on the cause.
items.body:
ATLANTA — Elon Musk was on the front row at Donald Trump’s second inauguration and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help the Republican president and his “Make America Great Again” allies win elections.

Now, after Republicans’ midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world’s richest man insists he’s not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels “pretty foolish” for spending so much money on the cause.

“I mean, I’m not MAGA,” Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday during the newspaper’s DealBook Summit.

“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” Musk continued, “but I, I don’t think I’m, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties.”

Musk, who has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, spent more than $400 million on Trump-aligned Republicans running in November. That included around $200 million backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico.

Democrats scored sweeping victories after making Musk, other tech titans and the proliferation of artificial intelligence and AI data centers a feature of the midterm campaigns. Their party will take control of Congress and many more U.S. statehouses in January, with a promise of a regulatory crackdown and congressional investigations into tech firms’ dealings with the Trump administration.

That leaves Musk and others scrambling to rebrand themselves after spending years aligning closely with Trump and his fellow Republicans as they sought government contracts and favorable policies on everything from taxation to AI regulation.

Palantir co-founder and CEO Alex Karp, whose software is used by the Pentagon, among his lucrative government portfolio, earlier this month raised eyebrows when he insisted to Politico that he’s always been a progressive.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment,” he said. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir -- all of our products are essentially progressive.”

Karp, a donor to Trump’s White House ballroom project who has adopted the president’s rhetoric to describe his own business as “anti-woke,” said he’s willing to support a Democrat for president in 2028.

At the Times’ event, Musk said if he had a do-over, he “probably” would have “spent less money” on the midterms.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk told columnist Andrew Sorkin. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”

Musk sat alongside other Big Tech billionaires at Trump’s inauguration and led the president’s Department of Government Efficiency, a post that for months made him the most high-profile figure in the administration other than Trump himself.

Hours after Trump was sworn in on Jan. 20, 2025, Musk appeared at a Trump rally in Washington, where he enthusiastically embraced the president’s agenda and his supporters.

“This was no ordinary victory,” he said. “This was a fork in the road of human civilization. OK? There are elections that come and go. Some elections are important, some are not. But this one really mattered. ... It is thanks to you that the future of civilization is assured.”

Some Democrats were unimpressed with Musk’s change in tenor.

Responding to Musk’s turnabout on X, the social media platform that Musk owns, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona was concise: “You are still getting a subpoena.”

Bill Barrow, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: The City of Ottawa says grocery giant Loblaw received a warning for unauthorized advertisements for its AI chatbot that appeared on local sidewalks.
items.body:
The City of Ottawa says grocery giant Loblaw received a warning for unauthorized advertisements for its AI chatbot that appeared on local sidewalks.

Advertisements for the PC Health app showed up on sidewalks around downtown Ottawa in early October, prompting criticism from residents. The City of Ottawa confirmed that the markings were not authorized and would be removed.

A spokesperson for Loblaw said at the time that the ad campaign used “an eco-friendly chalk” that would “wash off with water” and that it was intended to be a “creative and unexpected way” to show off its new app. It came shortly after Loblaw faced backlash for a late night drone show in Toronto to advertise the app.

While the City of Ottawa’s graffiti bylaw includes fines, none were levied in this case.

“Bylaw and Regulatory Services (BLRS) conducted an investigation with respect to the painted markings that were applied to sidewalks across Ottawa. BLRS follows a progressive enforcement model and provided education and a warning, and the markings have since been removed,” said Acting Chief of Bylaw and Regulatory Services Myrka Khorrami in a statement.

Loblaw said that it would clean up the markings after being told that the city considered the ads unauthorized.

“While chalk marketing activations are common in many communities, we’re working with our vendor to have the sidewalk markings removed as soon as possible,” Loblaw said in an email on Oct 7.

This was not the first time that ads like this caused controversy in Ottawa.

In 2019, several advertisements for Disney’s “The Lion King” appeared on sidewalks and pathways in the city, including some National Capital Commission paths.

The City of Ottawa said at the time that proper protocols were not followed for the advertisements.

items.title: Toronto commercial real estate investment already outpaces 2025
items.description: Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore
items.content: <p>Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307039780020741.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore
items.body:
Toronto commercial real estate investment has already surpassed its full-year 2025 total. Nearly $13.5 billion in transactions closed across the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) in the first nine months of 2026, according to Avison Young’s Greater Toronto investment review for the third quarter. That total is up 55% from the same period last year.

Third-quarter volume reached $4.4 billion, a 52% gain from Q3 2025, though 22% below a stronger second quarter. The number of trades rose a more modest 16% year to date, to 1,356.

“The much larger rise in dollar volume versus number of transactions is indicative of the increasing occurrence of large deals in the market,” the report said.

Multifamily leads as office capital returns

Multifamily was the quarter’s largest asset class at just over $1.7 billion, or 39% of total volume, up 310% year over year. Welltower Inc.’s $414 million purchase of a seniors’ housing portfolio from Amica Senior Lifestyles anchored the quarter.

Office posted the sharpest turnaround, with investment up 278% to $777 million. The largest deal was GWL Realty Advisors’ $243.6 million acquisition of 123 Front St. W. in Toronto from Oxford Properties. GTA-wide office availability fell 190 basis points from a year earlier to 17.6%.

“The improvements in the leasing market have allowed lenders to approach office assets with less apprehension (although this is still submarket- and asset-specific),” the report said.

“With tenant demand rising and little to no new supply in the development pipeline across downtown and suburban markets, investors’ view of the value of existing assets is increasing.”

Damon Conrad, vice-president at REMAX Canada Commercial, flagged the quality divide when investors flooding back to Toronto’s office sector first made headlines this year.

“I think office is seeing clear separation between premium amenity-rich buildings and the older assets that need repositioning,” Conrad told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

Industrial was the laggard. Volume fell 22% to $1.2 billion, and for the first time since Q3 2023, it was not the GTA’s most-traded asset class.

Rate hike tests lender appetite

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on Oct. 28, its first increase since July 2023. Avison Young warned that higher borrowing costs could affect how investors view asset values.

“With signs that both Canada and the US may continue to raise interest rates to combat inflation, there is the possibility that higher borrowing costs could impact investors’ views on asset values and demand for commercial real estate,” the report said.

The average multifamily capitalization rate, the ratio of a property’s net operating income to its sale price, rose 15 basis points to 4.09%.

“Nevertheless, traditional banks and funding sources are still actively seeking lending opportunities, and the situation surrounding tariffs and petroleum supply continues to evolve – with knock-on effects for the Canadian economy and real estate markets,” the report said.

Richard Joy, executive director at the Urban Land Institute in Toronto, has described an uneven recovery, a theme behind equity shortages threatening Canadian commercial refinancing in 2027.

“The GTA’s real estate market is moving at different speeds. Industrial and premium office show signs of recovery, while condominiums remain challenged,” Joy said.

“Investors remain cautious yet generally optimistic heading into the final months of the year,” the report said.

Avison Young expects strong activity in the fourth quarter.

items.title: Bargis: why CIMBC is backing the Canadian Mortgage Awards again
items.description: Coalition’s founder and chief executive officer highlights commitment to brokers, looks ahead to 2027 as CMAs draw closer
items.content: <p>Coalition’s founder and chief executive officer highlights commitment to brokers, looks ahead to 2027 as CMAs draw closer</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639307027915691028.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Coalition’s founder and chief executive officer highlights commitment to brokers, looks ahead to 2027 as CMAs draw closer
items.body:
The Coalition of Independent Mortgage Brokers of Canada (CIMBC) is returning as event partner for next week’s Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs), which mark their 20th year on November 25 at Rebel Toronto.

For John Bargis, the company’s founder and chief executive officer, that support represents an important symbol at a time when mortgage brokers are more important to the homebuying process than ever.

Bargis noted that CIMBC has backed the awards for years and said it was proud to step up again in 2026. “We couldn’t think of a better place to recognize our industry’s accomplishments and awards, and we look forward to a great evening of celebration,” he said.

Excellence Awardees are up for honours in 23 shortlisted categories at Wednesday’s ceremony, with hundreds of industry professionals set to gather from across the country to toast the sector’s best and brightest.

Bargis highlighted the importance of spotlighting the industry’s top performers. “Recognizing excellence matters in any industry because it highlights professionals and innovators who go above and beyond to lead meaningful change,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“When we celebrate those who truly elevate standards, we raise the bar for all of us that ultimately makes a difference where it counts the most: consumer confidence.”

This year’s ceremony arrives at an important moment for the mortgage market, which has struggled in recent years under the weight of higher interest rates, tariff-driven economic uncertainty, and affordability hurdles in many markets.

Still, that’s not to say the current downturn is unprecedented – and Bargis said he usually takes a long view of market cycles as they play out. “As an industry veteran, I’m often asked whether I’ve ever seen market conditions this challenging,” he said.

“My answer has always been: absolutely, I’ve seen a lot worse. But it doesn’t end there. Markets move in ebbs and flows. Our job is to recognize the opportunities in each cycle and make the adjustments needed to build a sustainable business, rather than chase the same deal as everyone else.”

In that environment, Bargis says he’s advised many CIMBC broker-owners and producing agents on building profitable business plans, including on regulatory and technology changes.

“All they have to do is be willing to step out of their comfort zone and make the necessary changes,” he said. “For those who choose not to, the alternative is far worse – especially in today’s market.”

The outlook for 2027’s mortgage market remains unclear. The Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, with expectations of further rate increases growing as inflation concerns persist.

That rising-rate environment could continue to put the squeeze on borrowers, and Bargis isn’t expecting a big rebound for the housing market. Still, he said there’s opportunity for those who search for it.

“For 2027, unfortunately, all economic indicators point to more of the same,” he said. “That doesn’t mean it’s all bad for those willing to pivot and rethink their business model, something I’ve had to do constantly to stay ahead of the curve.

“We’ve gone from a very robust market to one of more normalcy and stability that will take time to settle. Focus on making the necessary changes and you’ll come through it. Failure to do so will very likely yield unfavourable consequences.”

What CIMBC is prioritizing in the current market

CIMBC is a national coalition of independent, branded brokerages – and Bargis said his priority this year has been making sure the needs of members are met.

“As head of CIMBC, my main focus has been the continued success of our 90-plus independent brokerage brands across the country,” he said.

That work centres on partnerships and education. “We do that by building new strategic lender and industry partnerships and strengthening existing ones, all to improve our brokers’ long-term competitiveness and profitability,” he said. “We also point out growth opportunities, which is critical in slower and more challenging market conditions.”

Why CIMBC stays out of the awards running

The fact that CIMBC doesn’t put itself forward for the Network of the Year award is a deliberate decision by the coalition, Bargis said, consistent over years of backing the event.

“Though often referred to as one, CIMBC is not a network, so it makes no sense for us to be nominated in a category that doesn’t describe our structure or philosophy.”

He pointed to the optics of sponsoring the gala. “As title sponsor of this prestigious gala on a number of occasions, I’m sure you can also appreciate that optically it wouldn’t look right for us to be in the running for an award,” he said. “We’re just happy to be part of it all, and to be showcased throughout the evening by an organization that knows how to put on a great show.”

Bargis highlighted the strong performance of CIMBC’s model over the years, one he believes it would be difficult for others to emulate.

“The greatest compliment to CIMBC’s success, and proof of concept, is that some have recently tried to replicate our model,” he said. “To that, I say: ‘They can imitate, but it’s tough to duplicate.’”

items.description: Anthropic has raised US$81.3 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record after increasing the size of its offering, in a deal that values the Claude chatbot maker at $1.5 trillion and defied concerns over AI and tech fundraising.

(AP Photo/Andres Kudacki)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Andres Kudacki</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Anthropic has raised US$81.3 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record after increasing the size of its offering, in a deal that values the Claude chatbot maker at $1.5 trillion and defied concerns over AI and tech fundraising.
items.body:
Anthropic has raised US$81.3 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record after increasing the size of its offering, in a deal that values the Claude chatbot maker at $1.5 trillion and defied concerns over AI and tech fundraising.

In a sign of strong investor demand, Anthropic priced its shares at $83 each, above its initial range of $70 to $78.

Reuters was first to report on Wednesday that Anthropic, the first major frontier AI model developer to float, had increased the number of shares it was selling by about 19 per cent to 980 million.

Anthropic’s IPO eclipses the record-setting debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. Its total deal size is $107.3 billion, including another $26 billion that Anthropic is raising through a private placement of shares, the filings showed.

Nasdaq futures rose nearly 2 per cent on Thursday, bolstering expectations for a strong Anthropic debut and reviving sentiment around AI stocks.

Chipmakers and cloud companies, which have raised hundreds of billions of dollars to fund their massive spending plans, have in recent weeks come under pressure due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden exit of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

Anthropic has, meanwhile, faced questions about its outlook and ability to sustain rapid growth as competition intensifies.

Shares in Anthropic were up about 20 per cent in over-the-counter grey market trading, brokerages IG Markets and CMC Markets said.

“Volumes are big,” said Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets in Singapore, adding that the brokerage was “seeing demand from all clients, retail to institutional” for the grey market stocks.

Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder of Minotaur Capital, which is awaiting a share allocation, said the Anthropic IPO was a useful gauge of investor appetite for AI.

“But one listing won’t settle the debate. There’s a genuine wall of worry right now, and it’ll take a few things to climb it. Once Anthropic reports publicly, it becomes one of the clearest tests of whether the economics of AI are holding up.”

On a fully diluted basis, Anthropic’s IPO values it at about $1.5 trillion, including securities such as stock options and restricted stock, and on a non-diluted basis at about $1.1 trillion.

U.S. stock futures were up after Anthropic’s IPO details were made public, while Asian tech stocks remained under pressure amid broader concerns about the AI trade. Anthropic is set to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

A strong debut could give confidence to other companies waiting to tap public markets. Anthropic’s closest rival, OpenAI, is expected to pursue a listing as early as next year.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are lead underwriters for Anthropic’s IPO, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate, and were also lead underwriters for SpaceX’s listing.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Spending commitments expose risks

Anthropic’s growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers. Its annualized revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30, according to its IPO filing.

Underscoring its growing business foothold, Anthropic said it had 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of September 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year.

But to sustain that growth, Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier.

It also incurred an additional $5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity.

Revenue rose to $16.96 billion in the third quarter, up 47 per cent from the second. The company reported an operating loss of $567 million, compared with operating income of $974 million in the previous quarter.

The net loss narrowed to $23.3 billion from $66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating ​items related to bonds convertible into its shares.

Anthropic has committed to nearly $900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners, including Amazon and Alphabet’s Google, to train and operate AI models.

It warned that its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity.

“If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered,” Anthropic said in an IPO filing.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Competition and safety challenges

Anthropic faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety.

CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society’s ability to manage the risks.

“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” Anthropic said in the filing.

At the same time, competition is intensifying to be the leading provider of AI tools for businesses.

GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s latest flagship AI model, accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8 per cent for Claude Fable, data cited by Reuters in September showed.

The competitive threat extends beyond the handful of companies developing the most powerful commercial models. A recent Capgemini study found 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase their use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets.

Meta Platforms, one of Anthropic’s largest customers, has been looking to reduce its use of Anthropic’s models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, Reuters previously reported.

“Our thesis is that the vast amount of value will accrue to whoever is at the frontier,” said Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly $1.5 billion in Anthropic before its IPO.

“Our bet is that Anthropic has the ingredients — that doesn’t guarantee, but means that they arguably have the highest probability of remaining at the frontier.”

items.title: Canadian mortgage affordability worsens in all 13 major cities
items.description: Rising fixed rates push qualifying income higher across Canada’s biggest housing markets
items.content: <p>Rising fixed rates push qualifying income higher across Canada’s biggest housing markets</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639306974472710524.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rising fixed rates push qualifying income higher across Canada’s biggest housing markets
items.body:
Rising mortgage rates pushed home affordability lower across every major Canadian city in October.

Ratehub.ca’s Home Affordability Report found that buyers in all 13 markets studied needed more qualifying income than the month before, undoing the brief stabilisation affordability had briefly found its footing in September.

The deterioration was driven by rate movements, not prices. The average five-year fixed mortgage rate among Canada’s Big Five banks climbed 43 basis points, from 4.56% in September to 4.99% in October.

Home prices softened in eight of the 13 cities studied, but nowhere by enough to offset the cost of higher borrowing.

Bond yields drive qualifying income higher across Canada

Hamilton, Ontario, saw the sharpest decline.

“Based on our analysis, a borrower would require an additional $7,460 in income to purchase an average-priced home in the city. This was due to a significant rise in mortgage rates (+43 basis points) as well as a $10,300 increase in the local average home price,” Clay Jarvis, mortgage expert at Ratehub.ca in Toronto, explained.

“The Hamilton home buyer in this scenario would pay $217 dollars more on their monthly mortgage payment, or $2,604 per year, if they bought in October rather than September.”

Toronto buyers faced a $6,680 rise in required annual income; Vancouver, $6,650. Halifax, Montréal, and Victoria also recorded increases between $6,050 and $6,680. Edmonton saw the smallest change, at $1,970.

Jarvis identified bond markets as the central pressure point.

“Rates faced constant upward pressure due to elevated bond yields, which were pushed higher by high oil prices and heightened inflation expectations. While most cities saw home prices soften, the declines weren’t enough to offset the impact of higher mortgage rates and stress test qualifying rate.”

What the rate picture means for buyers and brokers

The Bank of Canada’s third-quarter Market Participants Survey results found that 52% of financial market professionals now view rate risks as skewed upward, with the median five-year Government of Canada bond yield forecast rising 35 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.50%.

The best available five-year fixed rate recently dipped 10 basis points to 4.34%, while the best variable rate stood at 3.65% as of November 18, according to Ratehub.ca.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Toronto, warned at the Women in Mortgage Summit Canada in September that fixed rates are likely heading higher still.

“It is a time when we should encourage anyone that is interested in potentially buying a home that they get pre-approved, because today’s rates, even though they’re a little above what they were last week and the week before, they’re only going higher,” Cooper said.

She added: “We have to expect higher interest rates, which also means that fixed-rate mortgages are very attractive now.”

Home sales fell 0.3% from September and were 10.6% lower year-over-year, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

With the average national sale price just 1.6% below year-ago levels, price declines alone cannot restore the affordability lost to higher rates.

items.title: Tax-loss selling – when does it make sense to sell at a loss?: Stan Wong
items.description: When I review a stock that’s down, I look at what’s changed in the earnings outlook, what the lower price already reflects and where else I could put the money. If the case for owning it has weakened, it may be time to sell.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A T1 General tax form is shown in this file photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Graeme Roy]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: When I review a stock that’s down, I look at what’s changed in the earnings outlook, what the lower price already reflects and where else I could put the money. If the case for owning it has weakened, it may be time to sell.
items.body:
A stock you bought at $50 now trades at $35. If you had the cash today, would you buy it at $35?

When I review a stock that’s down, I look at what’s changed in the earnings outlook, what the lower price already reflects and where else I could put the money. If the case for owning it has weakened, it may be time to sell.

If you’ve decided to sell, the loss may still be worth something at tax time. If you hold the stock in a non-registered account, you can generally use the realized loss to offset capital gains. Losses inside a TFSA, RRSP or other registered account can’t be used this way.

Why year-end timing matters

To use a loss against this year’s gains, the sale must settle before year-end.

Wednesday, Dec. 30, 2026, is the last trading day to sell most stocks and ETFs listed in Canada (TSX and TSX Venture) or the U.S. (NYSE and Nasdaq) for a sale to count in the 2026 Canadian tax year.

These trades normally settle one business day later, on Thursday, Dec. 31.

Work out what the loss can offset

Suppose you realized a $20,000 capital gain earlier this year. You then sell another investment in a non-registered account for an $8,000 capital loss. That brings your net capital gain to $12,000 before applying the capital gains inclusion rate.

If your capital losses exceed your gains this year, you can generally carry the net capital loss back to offset taxable capital gains from any of the previous three years or carry it forward indefinitely.

For a loss realized in 2026, that means looking back at 2023, 2024 and 2025. A gain from selling a cottage or rental property may be easy to overlook when you’re focused on your brokerage statement.

Confirm you have a loss in Canadian dollars

A U.S. stock can fall five per cent and still leave you with a capital gain in Canadian dollars. Say you bought it at US$100 when one U.S. dollar was worth $1.30, then sold it at US$95 when the exchange rate was $1.40. Your cost was $130 and your proceeds were $133 per share, leaving a small capital gain before trading costs.

Before placing a trade, verify the investment’s adjusted cost base. If you bought the same stock at different prices, generally use the weighted average across your non-registered accounts.

Look across accounts before you sell

Canada’s superficial loss rule can deny the loss if you or an affiliated person, such as your spouse or common-law partner, buys the same or an identical investment within 30 calendar days before or after the sale, and either of you still owns it 30 days after the sale.

Check both partners’ accounts for recent trades and scheduled purchases, including dividend reinvestments.

If you contribute an investment at a loss directly from a non-registered account to your TFSA or RRSP, you give up the capital loss. Selling it first and contributing cash, if you have contribution room, can preserve the loss, provided the superficial loss rule doesn’t apply.

Keep the exposure you still want

If you sell a stock at a loss but still see opportunity in its industry, you could reinvest the proceeds in a peer with a similar business. Consider whether its earnings outlook and valuation justify the purchase.

You could also buy a diversified sector ETF that holds the stock you sold. That would give you some exposure if the original stock rebounds while spreading the investment across several companies.

A Canadian depositary receipt (CDR), however, represents a direct interest in the underlying shares. If those are the same shares you sold, the CDR can be treated as identical property and trigger the superficial loss rule.

Tax-loss selling can be part of a total wealth plan, whether you’re trimming a concentrated position or raising cash for a planned expense. Your tax advisor can help you assess the value of the loss, and your wealth advisor can help you decide where the proceeds would serve you best.

If you’re still weighing whether to sell, start where we began. Would you buy the stock at today’s price?

items.title: Start with the problem, not the tech: how brokers should adopt AI
items.description: Fintech consultancy founder on the steps brokers need to take
items.content: <p>Fintech consultancy founder on the steps brokers need to take</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639306290579590103.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Fintech consultancy founder on the steps brokers need to take
items.body:
Artificial intelligence is a hot topic for mortgage brokers – but should they adopt technology for its own sake? Alfred Yang, founder of fintech consultancy Finnovate.io, told CMP about the steps brokers should be taking to bring AI into their brokerage.

[00:00] Aldred Young: Certainly, brokers are not going to be replaced by AI. As a homeowner myself, right? I prefer to talk to a human being and get, you know, sound advice.

[00:18] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, next up in our day two series of interviews at Markets Fest, we're joined by Aldred Young, who is the founder of Fin Innovate. Aldred, great to have you at the event. So, what are the main messages that you're bringing to brokers and members of the industry about the service that Fin Innovate is providing?

[00:34] Aldred Young: Yeah. So, fininnovate.io, we're a FinTech consultancy. So, we help mortgage brokers and also lenders implement technology to help them accelerate business outcomes. So, everything from back office automation to enhancing their client experiences. So, at the end of the day, I think my message would be to think about how technology can address certain challenges in their business as opposed to just applying technology for the sake of applying technology. So, start with the problems they're seeing in their business and applying the right technologies to address those problems. So, the main message is really just start with the problem and go from there.

[01:18] Fergal McAlinden: It's really interesting. We've been talking about the rise of artificial intelligence in the industry over the past couple of years. I know that it's not necessarily a blanket solution for everything that brokers and other industry members have. That's getting your message as well, that tech is worth it.

[01:33] Aldred Young: Yeah. So, again, right? Start by identifying a business problem that could be a quick win for you if addressed by technology. AI is certainly interesting. It's certainly a hot topic at this conference today. I would say that there's a lot of potential. Like we've heard about automation with AI, summarizing documents with AI, helping with underwriting and lending decisions with AI. I mean, all those fairly salient use cases.

[02:02] We've seen in the industry rapid experimentation with AI. So, for example, any organization that runs ads knows that they need to constantly be tweaking and iterating on messages to consumers and to businesses. So AI could really accelerate the prototyping and the tweaking of the message that you're conveying to your clients. So, we're working with a few organizations today to adopt AI to do these type of rapid prototyping and AB tests to fine tune the message that they're conveying to the market, which in turn helps them accelerate business outcomes.

[02:45] Fergal McAlinden: What would you say to brokers or other industry members who maybe are a little bit skeptical about AI or not sure about using it in their business? We heard on a panel yesterday there were some, I guess, some doubts about AI in the industry. What do you think about that?

[02:58] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say start small, right? I think AI is a very powerful tool, but at the same time comes risks when you're exposing your data to these large language models. So I think it's important to find the bottlenecks in your business processes, find the bottlenecks in your customer acquisition funnel, and identify one part of it that could potentially be addressed with AI and start there, right?

[03:28] Maybe start with data that is not so sensitive about your clients and start with data that is unique to your organization, but at the same time non-sensitive to your clients. Start there, start small, test it out and get some quick wins.

[03:46] Fergal McAlinden: Are there any trends that maybe aren't as prominent at the moment, but you think will be a big factor in the mortgage space in the next months and years ahead?

[03:54] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say there's opportunity in both the back office automation, like with KYC, with fraud detection, with automating underwriting decisions. I think there's huge opportunity in the back office, but at the same time on the customer acquisition side, like I said before, there's immense opportunity for you to automate and test your messages to the market using AI, just rapidly prototyping with human feedback in the loop.

[04:28] Fergal McAlinden: I heard a good line yesterday on one of the panels that brokers won't be replaced by AI, but brokers that don't use it might be replaced by brokers that do use it. So the importance of adopting it is really paramount.

[04:40] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say certainly brokers are not going to be replaced by AI because, as a homeowner myself, right, I'd prefer to talk to a human being and get sound advice, but I think AI can take a lot of the mundane work out of a broker's preparation before speaking to a client. All the document collection, all the boring tasks. Basically, automation allows brokers to free up much of their time and spend more time with their clients.

[05:14] Like AI can certainly help and elevate the client experience, but it certainly wouldn't replace the broker.

[05:21] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Well, any last message that you'd like to share or anything else that you're excited to announce you're working on?

[05:27] Aldred Young: Yeah, I would say we're excited about the prospect of the rapid advancement in technology and see how it would accelerate businesses not just in lending, but in wealth management, in financial services in general. And we're happy to be a part of it and we love to talk to anyone who feels like technology could help their business and we'd love to have a conversation.

[05:54] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Okay, well, great to talk to you today. Enjoy the rest of the show and we'll talk to you soon.

[05:58] Aldred Young: Yeah, thank you so much.

items.body:
OTTAWA — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.

The Liberals campaigned during the 2025 election on a pledge to double the annual pace of housing starts to roughly 500,000 over a decade.

But that promise was absent from the federal budget tabled on Nov. 5. The Liberal government instead set new goals in Budget 2026 to triple the pace of non-market housing construction over the next decade and to end homelessness.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan noted the missing reference to doubling home construction in a series of reports analyzing the budget published Tuesday.

"While Budget 2026 announces new measures for homelessness and housing affordability, it is not on track to double housing starts per Budget 2025, with year-to-date housing starts 4 per cent lower in 2026 than 2025," one of Ryan's report read.

The Canadian Press asked Robertson's office last week whether the Liberals were sticking to the target. A spokesperson for his office pointed to a statement sent to The Canadian Press six months earlier reaffirming the pledge.

Reporters asked Robertson as he was heading into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday if the government is sticking to the pledge it campaigned on a year and a half ago.

"We're just focused on supply overall for the time being. Affordable supply first and foremost," he said in response.

Robertson said the goal of doubling housing starts was based on the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp.'s estimates of the supply gap, or the number of homes the country needed to add to restore affordability to 2019 levels.

Hitting that annual pace requires the private sector to build at scale, he said, adding the government is "doing everything" it can to stabilize markets like Toronto and Vancouver that are struggling to get shovels in the ground.

The minister said the government has made "unprecedented" interventions to stimulate construction, including moves to axe the GST on many newly built units and other federal incentives to get municipalities to lower costly development charges.

But "the Government of Canada cannot force Canadians to build housing," he said.

"Right now we're doing everything that we can in a very challenging time for our economy," Robertson said.

"We have to continue focusing on where we intervene, working with provinces and cities to get them building as much as possible and looking at the affordable side. That's where the role of government is, to make sure there's affordable housing getting built."

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built — but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

Conservative housing critic Scott Aitchison accused the Liberals of quietly dropping their homebuilding target and moving the goalposts.

"Their big promises have become another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not make homes affordable again," he said in a media statement on Tuesday.

In its fall housing supply report, the CMHC wrote that the country is entering a "new phase" where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The CMHC's "business-as-usual" forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the CMHC said.

Experts point out that many of the levers to increase housing supply are outside the government's direct control, such as Bank of Canada interest rates and the cost of building materials.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, told The Canadian Press last week that he never liked the goal of doubling housing starts because it could be "excessive" and lacks a nuanced approach to the mix of homes Canada must build.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The Canadian real estate correction is already the largest in history, and gets even bigger after inflation. It's not over, according to BMO.
items.body:
Canadian real estate’s historic price correction is slowing down, but the pain may not be over. In a research note to investors, BMO Capital Markets explains it’s even larger in real terms. The banks warn that the math doesn’t work out in favour of households, who are still struggling with affordability. Combined with the recent upward pressure on interest rates, they see real home prices falling further for at least another year.

Canadian Home Price Declines Slowing After Historic Drop

The historic correction for Canadian home prices isn’t over, but it is losing steam. Price declines are getting smaller, with another bank even declaring the bottom. “Canadian home prices appear to be nearly flattening out in nominal terms, but the adjustment is ongoing after accounting for inflation—and we suspect it will continue,” says BMO Economist Robert Kavcic.

The latest national benchmark from CREA shows a typical home has shed 22.8% (-$191.6k) from the March 2022 peak. In the past year, the benchmark fell 3.1% (-$20.7k), a relatively small move in contrast to the $649.9k benchmark. However, those declines are in nominal terms. In real (inflation-adjusted) terms, the market is a whole different story.

Canadians Have Seen Inflation Run Hot—and It’s Not Slowing Down

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) report shows prices are 3.1% higher than last year, over 50% higher than the BoC target. Consumer prices have grown 19.9% from 2020 to 2025, or 3.7% annualized over the 5 years. Significantly outpacing the target inflation rate means stronger depreciation in real terms.

“Real Canadian home prices are down 4.7% from a year ago after inflation, and are now down a massive 20% from five years ago— that’s the steepest five-year real decline on record going back to the start of the 1980s,” notes Kavcic.

Canadian Home Prices Not Expected To Rise Through 2030

Inflation-adjusted average Canadian home price.

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

One may assume the sharpest drop in history means the market is ready to return? Not exactly.

“Given where valuations still sit relative to income and rent, and assuming that interest rates are nudging higher rather than headed lower, there is simply no scope for price increases to run ahead of inflation at this stage,” warns Kavcic.

He’s not outright dismissing the possibility of an uptick in home prices. The math is just working against it, especially when it comes to real terms.

“Thus, even if nominal prices turn the corner, the adjustment relative to inflation (and, similarly, relative to household income) will continue in the year (or more) ahead,” warns Kavcic.

items.title: Canadian consumer confidence stalls as homeowners grow more cautious
items.description: Homeowner mood dips in Nanos data weeks after the Bank of Canada rate increase
items.content: <p>Homeowner mood dips in Nanos data weeks after the Bank of Canada rate increase</p><img src="https://ca.res.keymedia.com/files/image/iStock-housinghomemortgage(500%20x%20333).jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Homeowner mood dips in Nanos data weeks after the Bank of Canada rate increase
items.body:
Canadian consumer confidence spent the past month going nowhere, and the latest data suggest homeowners are now less upbeat than the renters down the street.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index (BNCCI) registered 51.54 for the four weeks ending November 13. That was barely changed from 51.68 a month earlier and well short of its 54.64 average since tracking began in 2008, according to Nanos Research Corporation.

A reading of 50 means positive and negative views cancel each other out.

The tracking window included the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision to lift its overnight rate to 2.5%. It was the central bank’s first increase since 2023. A year ago, the index sat at 48.63. 

What the housing outlook means for mortgage brokers

Roughly 32% of Canadians expect home values in their neighbourhood to rise over the next six months. That is up from 29% four weeks earlier but below this year’s 34% average and the 40% long-run norm. Another 21% expect prices to fall.

The Expectations Index, which blends views on the economy and real estate, sat at 48.75, still net negative.

That caution matches recent bank forecasts. TD expects home sales and prices to decline through the fourth quarter. Economist Rishi Sondhi warned that “the risk is that November is another subdued month for housing.” 

The broader index briefly slipped below the neutral mark in September before recovering in October. It has averaged 51.06 so far in 2026, according to Nanos.

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

Why are homeowners less confident than renters?

Sentiment among homeowners slipped to 50.14 from 51.64 four weeks earlier, edging toward net-negative territory. Renters climbed to 54.81 from 51.90 over the same period.

Ontario scored 49.57 and the Prairies came in at 49.81, the only two regions below neutral. British Columbia moved the other way, jumping to 53.56 from 46.02 four weeks earlier. Quebec posted the strongest regional reading at 53.70.

Household balance sheets remain the weak spot. Only 9% of respondents said their personal finances improved over the past year, against 42% who said they were worse off.

Job security held up better, with 66% describing their work as secure or somewhat secure, above the 2026 average of 63%. Fewer than 6% said their jobs were not secure at all or somewhat not secure.

How Canadians see their neighbourhood housing market

Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index, four weeks ending November 13, 2026

Source: Nanos Research for Bloomberg; random telephone survey of 1,019 Canadians aged 18 and over, four-week rolling average ending November 13, 2026. Margin of error ±3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

items._ogDesc: Western Canada's mortgage industry gathers in Vancouver in February for its annual summit
items.body:
Vancouver Convention Centre will play host to the Canadian Mortgage Summit Vancouver on February 25, 2027, as mortgage brokers, lenders, underwriters, and industry service providers from across Western Canada converge for a full day of market intelligence, business strategy, and lending solutions.

The event marks the latest edition of a conference series built specifically around the challenges and opportunities facing mortgage professionals in British Columbia and the broader western region.

A market in transition

The timing of the 2027 summit reflects the conditions reshaping Canadian mortgage brokering. Broker market share has climbed to 33% of new residential mortgage originations, up four percentage points since the end of 2022, according to CMP's 2026 Brokers on Lenders report.

The program has been designed to address this environment directly. The agenda is organised around four themes:

  1. Market intelligence - covering changing conditions and borrower behaviour across Western Canada;
  2. Artificial intelligence and technology - examining how automation and digital tools can sharpen broker workflows;
  3. Business strategy and growth - focusing on adaptation and diversification in a tighter market;
  4. Lending solutions - exploring private, mortgage investment corporation (MIC), and alternative financing structures

Western Canada carries its own dynamics. British Columbia's housing market has been under consistent affordability pressure, and brokers operating in the province face a client base navigating some of Canada's highest property values alongside elevated interest rate sensitivity.

For the alternative lending sector in particular, British Columbia and Alberta represent two of the most active markets for private mortgage activity, a fact reflected in the sponsor roster assembled for the 2027 event.

Speakers and what attendees can expect

The confirmed speaker lineup spans origination, alternative lending, technology, and mortgage education.

Joe White, founder of Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) and IMBoundless, is among the featured presenters.

White, a Canadian Mortgage Professional Hall of Fame inductee, has trained more than 50,000 mortgage students and leads what the organization describes as Canada's largest mortgage and insurance education platform.

Jared Stanley, chief operating officer at Neighbourhood Holdings in British Columbia, will also appear. Stanley oversaw the alternative lender's growth to $2 billion in volume by April 2025 and has spoken publicly about the role of process automation and AI-assisted underwriting in scaling complex file management.

Neighbourhood Holdings completed the acquisition of Fisgard Asset Management in October 2025, a deal that positions the combined entity as one of Canada's larger alternative lenders.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthONE Bank of Canada, brings more than 20 years of mortgage and financial services experience to the program.

Armstrong leads origination strategy and broker channel development at WealthONE, which specializes in lending solutions for self-employed borrowers, multiple property owners, and newcomers to Canada — borrower profiles that represent a significant and growing share of broker deal flow in British Columbia.

Michael Wolfe, vice president of residential lending at EQ Bank (a subsidiary of Equitable Bank), and Ryan Spence, principal of broker channel development at Filogix, round out the confirmed roster, with additional speakers expected to be announced in the weeks ahead.

The Canadian Mortgage Summit Vancouver is currently accepting waitlist registrations ahead of a broader registration opening. Sponsorship opportunities remain available. 

Full event details and waitlist registration are available at vancouver.canadianmortgagesummit.com.

items.content: <p>Canada's largest mortgage educator on recognition, trust, and what the CMAs mean for the next generation</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639256797300291475.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada's largest mortgage educator on recognition, trust, and what the CMAs mean for the next generation
items.body:
Joe White (pictured top) has trained most of the people competing at this year's Canadian Mortgage Awards. The founder and chief executive of the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) in Toronto has licensed more than 20,000 mortgage professionals in Ontario alone since founding the company in 2008, and each year REMIC trains more than 15,000 students across financial services.

When the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards return to Rebel Toronto on November 25, marking the programme's 20th anniversary, many of the finalists will have started their careers in one of his classrooms.

Seeing the full journey

"When I look at the finalist list, I see a lot of people who started in one of our classrooms," White told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Sponsoring the awards lets us see that whole path, from the first day of licensing to standing on a stage being recognised by their peers."

The awards, presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, span 23 competitive categories this year, from individual broker performance to brokerage innovation and technology.

The ceremony will be hosted by broadcaster Sonia Mangat and winners will be announced the same night across CMP's channels.

REMIC is backing the FinFluencer of the Year award in particular, a category recognising brokers who build a public profile online and educate Canadian consumers about mortgages and financial products.

The recognition, he argues, sets a standard that advertising alone cannot. "When new agents see what excellence looks like, they have something to aim for," he said.

"And frankly, our industry needs to make the case for the value of professional, licensed advice now more than ever."

White sees the category as a natural fit for an organisation whose newest programs encourage licensees to establish a digital presence from the moment they qualify.

"The brokers who are building trust online and educating Canadians in public are doing work that matters," he said, "and they deserve a spotlight."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with RPS in recognizing the Excellence Awardees of the RPS Award for Brokerage/Team of the Year (25 Employees or More). #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/DpeOmLlH9a https://t.co/2TA4fmH933 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 17, 2026

Why recognition matters now

White's argument for the awards goes beyond ceremony. The public, he says, does not see what a skilled broker actually does — they see a rate.

They do not see the broker who salvaged a self-employed client's deal at nine in the evening, or the agent who talked a family out of a mortgage they could not afford. Recognition, he believes, corrects that.

"Because the public doesn't see what good brokers do," White said.

"Recognition sets the standard. When new agents see what excellence looks like, they have something to aim for. And frankly, our industry needs to make the case for the value of professional, licensed advice now more than ever."

That case is becoming more urgent. A national survey commissioned by REMIC and conducted by Abacus Data in June found that among Canadians aged 18 to 29, more had used AI tools for financial or mortgage advice in the past year — 26% — than had used a licensed mortgage broker or financial adviser — 17%.

Nearly half of all Canadians surveyed did not know whether AI mortgage advice was regulated. Trust still favours the licensed professional, but White is clear-eyed about the direction of travel.

The brokers most visible in 2027, he said, will be the ones who explain things clearly, show up where consumers are looking, and use technology to serve clients better.
